summary: Describes ISO-2022-JP-1, a way to encode Japanese characters for use in email and network news, and lists the characters in the set. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers need a code for each Japanese character. This is a code sheet for sending Japanese writing safely by email.

questions: how to encode japanese characters in email
how to encode japanese in email
subtitle: An encoding scheme for Japanese characters in email and network messages.

tldr.problem: Japanese text in email and network news required an encoding method, but the existing standard (RFC 1468, which used JIS X 0208) could not represent all Japanese characters, limiting communication precision.
tldr.mechanism: ISO-2022-JP-1 extends the earlier encoding by adding support for JIS X 0212, a supplementary Japanese character set, while remaining compatible with 7-bit email systems through escape sequences.
tldr.outcome: Messages can now encode a much broader range of Japanese characters, including rarely used Kanji, while maintaining compatibility with systems that only support the earlier encoding.

today: RFC 2237 is an Informational RFC describing a character encoding for Japanese text in email. It has not been obsoleted and remains a standard way to encode Japanese characters for systems that require 7-bit compatibility.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
RFC 1468 defined how to encode Japanese characters in email and network news using escape sequences and two character sets: JIS X 0201-Roman (for ASCII-like text) and JIS X 0208-1983 (for Japanese characters). However, many operating systems, Unicode, and the Japanese Industry Standard define JIS X 0212, a supplementary Japanese graphic character set containing additional Kanji characters not in JIS X 0208.

This RFC extends RFC 1468 by adding support for JIS X 0212 while maintaining backward compatibility. Systems that do not support JIS X 0212 can still send and receive text using only JIS X 0208 by following the original standard. Text that uses JIS X 0212 must be marked as ISO-2022-JP-1 rather than the older ISO-2022-JP encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: There was an old way to write Japanese in email, but it could not write all Japanese characters. This is an improved way that handles more characters.

sections.title: How ISO-2022-JP-1 Works
sections.content:
ISO-2022-JP-1 text starts in ASCII. Escape sequences (starting with the escape character followed by specific bytes) designate which character set is active. The sequence ESC $ B switches to JIS X 0208-1983 for double-byte characters. The sequence ESC $ ( D switches to JIS X 0212-1990. The sequence ESC ( B returns to ASCII or ESC ( J returns to JIS X 0201-Roman.

Text MUST begin in ASCII and MUST end in ASCII. It is strongly recommended to return to ASCII at the end of each line rather than staying in another character set. Each character set can encode two or more bytes per character. The RFC discourages the use of ESC $ @ (JIS X 0208-1978) because it is obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: The email starts in English mode. Special codes say 'switch to Japanese mode' or 'switch back to English'. Each code tells the computer which alphabet to use for the next characters.

sections.title: Compatibility and MIME Usage
sections.content:
ISO-2022-JP-1 is a 7-bit encoding, meaning it uses only ASCII characters (including control characters). All character sets—ASCII, JIS X 0208, JIS X 0212, and JIS X 0201-Roman—fit within 7-bit boundaries after escape sequences. This makes it suitable for email systems that cannot handle 8-bit data.

In MIME headers, ISO-2022-JP-1 is declared as Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-jp-1. No additional content transfer encoding (like Base64) is required, though it is permitted. For backward compatibility, implementers are strongly encouraged to also transmit text in the older ISO-2022-JP format in addition to ISO-2022-JP-1.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole message uses only basic computer letters and numbers, no special characters, so it works on old email systems. Modern systems should recognize both the old way and this new way.

sections.title: Character Sets and Escape Sequences
sections.content:
The RFC defines the formal grammar for valid ISO-2022-JP-1 text. Five character sets are available: ASCII (reg# 6, via ESC ( B), JIS X 0208-1978 (reg# 42, deprecated), JIS X 0208-1983 (reg# 87, via ESC $ B), JIS X 0201-Roman (reg# 14, via ESC ( J), and JIS X 0212-1990 (reg# 159, via ESC $ ( D). Each byte can represent values from 33 to 126 (the printable range of 7-bit ASCII).

A valid message consists of zero or more lines, each containing single-byte segments (ASCII or JIS X 0201-Roman) or double-byte segments (JIS X 0208 or JIS X 0212). Each line ends with CRLF. The message may optionally end with a final line without CRLF.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five different alphabets available, each turned on with a special code. Each line of the message ends with a carriage return and line feed.
